subject: Physics

buckets.title: Current electricity: charge-flow foundation
buckets.badge_reason: Charge conservation must be separated from energy-transfer language before circuit equations are introduced.

capabilities.action: Track steady charge flow across the two boundaries of one unbranched circuit element.
capabilities.success_criterion: Explain why steady current entering and leaving the element must match when charge is not accumulating inside it.

capabilities.action: Test whether measured voltage-current pairs support one constant-resistance model under fixed conditions.
capabilities.success_criterion: From a small set of voltage-current pairs, decide whether the voltage-to-current ratio stays constant and state whether the constant-resistance model is supported.

microtopics.title: Charge flow is not consumed by a component
microtopics.badge_reason: Everyday language about using electricity makes it easy to confuse energy transfer with disappearance of charge flow.
entry_assumptions: Can count charge carriers or total charge crossing a point over a time interval.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Current is a rate of charge passing a boundary; charge is not used up by a resistor.

teaching_path.action: Mark an entry boundary and an exit boundary around one component, and compare charge passage over matching time windows.
teaching_path.why_valid: Matching intervals make the two flow statements comparable; otherwise a difference could come only from observing for different lengths of time.
teaching_path.output: entry boundary = one count window; exit boundary = the same count window

teaching_path.action: Suppose the entry flow were persistently larger than the exit flow while the circuit stayed steady.
teaching_path.why_valid: The difference would have to remain inside the component as accumulating charge, so a permanent mismatch contradicts the stated steady condition.
teaching_path.output: more in than out -> charge pile-up; steady no-pile-up -> matching flow

teaching_path.action: Repeat the boundary comparison after replacing the component with a different ordinary component while keeping a single unbranched path.
teaching_path.why_valid: The conservation argument depends on the steady one-path condition, not on the component's particular construction.
teaching_path.output: single steady path -> same flow at entry and exit

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Current gets smaller after charge passes through a resistor.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: One ampere enters a resistor in a single unbranched path. In steady operation, what current leaves it?
misconceptions.repair: Track charge through the boundary: steady current cannot accumulate charge inside the resistor.

exit_task.prompt: A steady single-path circuit carries charge through one component. Say whether the charge-flow rate can be persistently smaller at the exit than at the entry and justify the answer without appealing to what the component does with energy.

answer.summary: It cannot be persistently smaller in the stated steady one-path case, because the missing charge would otherwise have to accumulate inside the component.
reasoning: Compare entry and exit over the same time window so the two flow statements refer to the same interval.
A sustained excess entering over leaving would increase the charge stored inside the component.
The stated steady condition excludes continuing accumulation, so the entry and exit flow rates must match.
answer.check: Ask where the difference would physically go if the two steady flow rates were unequal; if no accumulating store is allowed, the mismatch is inconsistent.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit answer is a conservation argument about equality of steady flow, not a computation of a numerical electrical quantity.

microtopics.research_contribution: This author-created boundary ledger isolates charge conservation from later energy and circuit-law relations so the low rung can be reviewed independently.

predict.prompt: If a lamp glows in a steady one-path circuit, should less charge per second leave the lamp than entered it?
predict.defensible_answer: No. A lasting difference would imply charge continuously collecting inside the lamp.

attempt.produces: A boundary ledger showing what crosses into and out of one component during the same interval, plus a sentence accounting for any proposed mismatch.

rubric.criterion: The entry and exit observations use the same time interval.
rubric.evidence_of: Making the two flow-rate claims comparable.

rubric.criterion: Any proposed mismatch is traced to charge accumulation inside the component.
rubric.evidence_of: Using conservation rather than the vague claim that current stays the same.

accepted: The ledger compares matching windows and says a persistent excess entering would pile charge up inside, so a steady case requires matching entry and exit flow.
rejected: The response says the component uses some current and therefore less leaves, but names no place where the missing charge accumulates.

route.ask: What two boundaries would you watch if you wanted to know whether charge disappeared inside the component?
route.why_this_ask: It turns a vague flow idea into a closed accounting region.

route.ask: If more charge keeps entering than leaving, what must happen inside that region over time?
route.why_this_ask: The consequence of the misconception is easier to test than the rule itself.

route.ask: Does changing the component remove that accounting requirement while the path remains single and steady?
route.why_this_ask: It tests whether the learner attached the result to conservation rather than to one device.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The declarative path presents the boundary ledger; the elicitation route begins with the learner's own consumption prediction and makes them locate the supposedly missing charge.

boundary_test.prompt: Could entry and exit flow differ briefly while charge is building up on part of a circuit?
boundary_test.answer: Yes. The steady-state conclusion does not forbid a transient interval in which charge distribution is still changing.
boundary_test.confirms: The conservation claim is tied to the stated steady condition rather than asserted as an exceptionless slogan.

microtopics.title: Ohmic behavior is a tested model, not a permanent label
microtopics.badge_reason: The learner must separate a measured proportional pattern from the stronger claim that every device keeps one resistance under every operating condition.
entry_assumptions: Can read paired voltage and current measurements for one device.
Can compare repeated ratios without treating a device name as evidence.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A constant-resistance Ohmic model is supported only when one device keeps the same voltage-to-current ratio across operating points while the relevant conditions are held fixed; changing the operating condition can make that model stop fitting.

teaching_path.action: Fix one device and one thermal condition, then place several measured voltage-current pairs in a table before naming any model.
teaching_path.why_valid: The model is a claim about a repeatable relationship under stated conditions, so device identity and condition must be held fixed before the measurements can test it.
teaching_path.output: same device + same thermal condition -> compare one V-I table

teaching_path.action: For the first table, divide each voltage by its paired current and compare the results.
teaching_path.why_valid: A single constant-resistance model predicts one unchanged proportionality across the measured operating points, so the repeated ratio is the direct test of that model.
teaching_path.output: 2/1 = 2 Ω; 4/2 = 2 Ω; 6/3 = 2 Ω -> one constant ratio

teaching_path.action: Repeat the same ratio check for a second table in which the device condition has changed, and refuse to carry the first model across automatically.
teaching_path.why_valid: Evidence collected under one condition does not authorize the same parameter under a changed condition; re-testing distinguishes a model from a permanent device label.
teaching_path.output: condition A: one ratio pattern; condition B: changed ratio pattern -> re-test the model

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Every electrical component has one fixed resistance, so a constant-resistance model always applies.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If doubling the voltage more than doubles the current, is one constant ratio enough to describe the device over those measurements?
misconceptions.repair: Use the measured voltage-current pattern first; keep one constant resistance only when the ratio stays unchanged under the stated fixed conditions.

exit_task.prompt: Two voltage-current tables come from devices tested under fixed conditions. In table A the voltage-to-current ratio stays the same across all measured points; in table B it changes. Decide which table supports one constant-resistance Ohmic model and state the evidence.

answer.summary: Table A supports the constant-resistance model because its voltage-to-current ratio is unchanged across the measurements; table B does not because that ratio changes.
reasoning: Treat each table as evidence rather than assuming a model from the device name.
Compare the voltage-to-current ratio across every operating point in the same table.
Keep the constant-resistance model only for the table whose ratio remains unchanged under the stated fixed conditions.
answer.check: A different pair from the same table should lead to the same model decision; if one pair changes the ratio pattern, the constant-resistance claim is not supported over the full set.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit answer classifies whether a constant-ratio model is supported; it reports no computed resistance value.

microtopics.research_contribution: This author-created measurement-first construction isolates the model-validity distinction in the matrix without importing an ungated circuit equation as a library relation.

predict.prompt: A component is called a resistor. Before seeing any measurements, is that name enough to prove one constant resistance describes it at every operating point?
predict.defensible_answer: No. The constant-resistance claim must be tested against measured voltage-current pairs under stated conditions.

attempt.produces: A model decision for each of two V-I tables, with the repeated-ratio evidence written beside the decision.

rubric.criterion: The decision is based on whether the voltage-to-current ratio stays constant across all listed pairs.
rubric.evidence_of: Testing the model against the whole measured pattern rather than one convenient point.

rubric.criterion: The stated fixed condition is kept attached to the conclusion.
rubric.evidence_of: Treating constant resistance as a conditional model rather than a permanent device property.

accepted: Table A supports one constant resistance because the same ratio pattern persists at every measured point under the fixed condition; table B does not because its ratio pattern changes.
rejected: Both tables are called Ohmic because each contains voltage and current values; no comparison across operating points is made.

route.ask: What must stay fixed before measurements from different operating points can test one model?
route.why_this_ask: It prevents a condition change from being mistaken for failure or success of the same model.

route.ask: What comparison can you repeat for every voltage-current pair without assuming the answer first?
route.why_this_ask: The learner discovers the proportionality test from the data rather than receiving a device label.

route.ask: If that comparison is unchanged in one table and changes in another, which table supports one constant parameter?
route.why_this_ask: This turns the numerical pattern into the model-choice claim the rung teaches.

route.ask: What should you do after the device temperature changes?
route.why_this_ask: The final ask tests whether the learner understands the stated condition as part of the model.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path starts with a declared measurement condition and performs the ratio test; the elicitation route first challenges the device-label shortcut and makes the learner identify what evidence could justify the model.

boundary_test.prompt: If only one voltage-current pair has been measured, can that single point establish that the ratio will remain constant as the operating point changes?
boundary_test.answer: No. One point can be fitted by a constant parameter, but it cannot show that the same parameter persists across other operating points.
boundary_test.confirms: The rung is about evidence for a relationship across conditions, not about attaching a resistance label from one measurement.

teaching_routes.title: Completed charge-flow ledger
entry_needs: Learners can count charge crossing a point during a stated interval.
learner_actions: Read a completed entry-and-exit boundary ledger.
Explain the accumulation consequence of unequal steady flow.
Test a completed V-I data set for a constant ratio before accepting a constant-resistance model.
help_plan: Keep the accounting region visible around one component.
Keep the device condition attached to the ratio test so the model is not generalized beyond its evidence.
teaching_routes.reveal_plan: The study route reveals the completed conservation argument and its steady-state boundary.

source_preferences.reason: The authored source supplies the boundary-ledger construction.

when_not_suitable: Do not extend this route into drift, voltage-definition, equivalent-resistance, power or loop equations without governed relations.

teaching_routes.title: Elicit the missing-charge contradiction
entry_needs: Learners can make a prediction about what enters and leaves a component.
learner_actions: Account for the missing charge if a mismatch is claimed.
Test the result against a transient boundary case.
Predict whether a device label alone justifies constant resistance, then reconstruct the repeated-ratio test from measurements.
help_plan: Ask where missing charge would go before revealing conservation.
Offer the boundary ledger only after the learner commits.
Ask what evidence would distinguish a model from a permanent device label before showing the ratio comparison.
teaching_routes.reveal_plan: The tutor lets the learner's consumption model create an accumulation contradiction before naming the repair.

source_preferences.reason: The authored resource holds the prompts and model closure.

when_not_suitable: Do not turn the elicitation into equivalent-resistance, power or Kirchhoff calculation practice without governed relations.
